questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: A coworker asks why bystander CPR matters when EMS will arrive in a few minutes anyway. Which statement best summarizes the impact of immediate high-quality CPR combined with early defibrillation on survival from cardiac arrest?

answers.text: It can double or triple the chances of survival
It improves survival by less than five percent in any setting
It only matters when the arrest happens inside a hospital
It has no effect until advanced life support arrives

explanations.a: AHA states that high-quality CPR started immediately after cardiac arrest combined with early defibrillation can double or triple the chances of survival.
explanations.b: Survival improvement is far greater than five percent — bystander CPR with defibrillation can multiply survival several-fold.
explanations.c: The benefit applies in both in-hospital and out-of-hospital settings; out-of-hospital arrests in particular depend on bystander action.
explanations.d: CPR and defibrillation are the foundation of survival; waiting for ALS without them dramatically lowers the chance of a good outcome.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: Your training partner says that almost everyone who has a cardiac arrest outside the hospital survives if EMS is called. According to the BLS Provider Manual, what is the approximate survival-to-discharge rate for adult nontraumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by EMS?

answers.text: Roughly 50 percent
Nearly 90 percent
Approximately 75 percent
About 10 percent

explanations.a: Survival is far lower than half — overstating it can give bystanders a false sense that early action does not matter.
explanations.b: Nine out of ten surviving would contradict the published reality that OHCA is a leading cause of death.
explanations.c: Three-quarters survival would imply OHCA is a minor problem; in reality outcomes remain poor, which is why early bystander action is critical.
explanations.d: The BLS Provider Manual reports that only about 10 percent of adults with nontraumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by EMS survive to hospital discharge.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: An instructor draws the AHA Chain of Survival on the board and asks the class to identify the very first link a rescuer acts on when someone collapses. Which link is it?

answers.text: Recognition and emergency activation
Advanced resuscitation
Defibrillation
Post-cardiac arrest care

explanations.a: Recognition and emergency activation is the first link — the rescuer recognizes the arrest and activates the emergency response system.
explanations.b: Advanced resuscitation occurs once a high-performance team has taken over, well after the first link.
explanations.c: Defibrillation is the third link, applied after recognition has triggered EMS activation and CPR has begun.
explanations.d: Post-cardiac arrest care follows return of spontaneous circulation, near the end of the chain rather than the beginning.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: You are reviewing the six AHA Chain of Survival links to teach a community CPR class. Which sequence places the links in the correct order from first to last?

answers.text: High-quality CPR, recognition, defibrillation, advanced resuscitation, recovery, post-arrest care
Recognition and activation, high-quality CPR, defibrillation, advanced resuscitation, post-cardiac arrest care, recovery and survivorship
Defibrillation, recognition, CPR, recovery, advanced resuscitation, post-arrest care
Recognition, defibrillation, CPR, post-arrest care, advanced resuscitation, recovery

explanations.a: High-quality CPR cannot precede recognition — you have to know an arrest is happening before compressions begin.
explanations.b: The AHA chain runs recognition and activation, high-quality CPR, defibrillation, advanced resuscitation, post-cardiac arrest care, then recovery and survivorship.
explanations.c: Defibrillation cannot precede recognition; rhythm cannot be analyzed before the AED is even called for.
explanations.d: Post-arrest care must follow advanced resuscitation, not precede it, because it begins after return of spontaneous circulation.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: An AHA fact sheet states that one element underlies the entire Chain of Survival rather than appearing as a single link. Which element does it describe in this way?

answers.text: Cardiac catheterization availability
Public access defibrillation
Rapid response team activation
Prevention of cardiac arrest

explanations.a: Cardiac catheterization is part of post-cardiac arrest care, not the foundation underlying every link.
explanations.b: Public access defibrillation supports the defibrillation link specifically rather than serving as the foundation of the chain.
explanations.c: Rapid response teams are an in-hospital tactic, not the foundation of the entire chain.
explanations.d: Per AHA Part 2, prevention of cardiac arrest is the foundation of the Chain of Survival, supported by public awareness, training, and emergency response system development.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: After confirming the scene is safe, you reach an adult lying motionless on the floor of a coffee shop. Which technique is the AHA-recommended way to check whether the adult is responsive?

answers.text: Sprinkle water on the face and watch for a flinch
Pinch the cheek firmly for ten seconds
Tap the shoulders and shout, 'Hey! Are you OK?'
Roll the person onto the side and listen for breathing

explanations.a: Splashing water is not a recognized AHA responsiveness check and only delays activation of the emergency response system.
explanations.b: Cheek-pinching is not part of the AHA assessment; it does not reliably distinguish responsive from unresponsive.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2 instructs rescuers to tap the adult's shoulders and shout, 'Hey! Are you OK?' to check responsiveness.
explanations.d: Rolling the person before assessing wastes time and can worsen any spinal injury; the check is done in place first.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: A daycare worker finds an unresponsive-appearing infant in a crib. After verifying the scene is safe, where should they tap to check the infant's responsiveness according to the AHA approach?

answers.text: On both shoulders, the same as for an adult
On the heel of the foot
On the forehead between the eyes
On the abdomen near the navel

explanations.a: Shoulder tap is used for adults and children; infants are checked at a different anatomic site per AHA guidance.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2 specifies tapping the infant's heel while shouting to assess responsiveness.
explanations.c: Tapping the forehead is not the recommended infant assessment point and may not produce a useful response.
explanations.d: Abdominal tapping is not part of the responsiveness check at any age.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: Your colleague argues you should always check breathing first and only then move on to the pulse. According to the AHA approach to minimize delays in starting CPR, what is the recommended way to assess these two findings?

answers.text: Check breathing first for thirty seconds, then start a separate pulse check
Skip the pulse check entirely for any adult
Assess breathing and pulse simultaneously for at least 5 but no more than 10 seconds
Check the pulse for 60 seconds before assessing breathing

explanations.a: A 30-second breathing check followed by a separate pulse check creates an unnecessary delay before starting compressions.
explanations.b: Health care providers do perform a pulse check; skipping it removes a key piece of information used to choose the next action.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2 instructs rescuers to assess breathing and pulse at the same time for at least 5 but no more than 10 seconds.
explanations.d: A 60-second pulse check would push the start of CPR well past the recommended threshold and lower the chance of survival.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: A community task force is planning to place AEDs in airports, schools, and convention centers, and to train laypeople in their use. Which AHA initiative does this approach describe?

answers.text: Telecommunicator-assisted CPR
Post-cardiac arrest neuroprognostication
A rapid response team
A public access defibrillation program

explanations.a: Telecommunicator-assisted CPR is dispatcher-guided phone instruction to a caller, not AED placement in public spaces.
explanations.b: Neuroprognostication is brain-recovery assessment after ROSC and has no role in placing AEDs in public areas.
explanations.c: A rapid response team is an in-hospital staffed team that responds to deteriorating patients, not a public AED program.
explanations.d: Public access defibrillation programs place AEDs where many people gather and train laypeople to use them, exactly matching this scenario.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: An untrained bystander calls 911 after a stranger collapses, and the emergency telecommunicator coaches the caller through chest compressions over the phone until EMS arrives. The BLS Provider Manual identifies this practice by which abbreviation?

answers.text: PAD
PALS
T-CPR
ROSC

explanations.a: PAD stands for public access defibrillation, which is about device placement, not phone-coached compressions.
explanations.b: PALS is pediatric advanced life support, an in-person clinical intervention rather than dispatcher coaching.
explanations.c: T-CPR is telecommunicator-assisted CPR, the dispatcher-guided coaching that helps untrained callers perform high-quality compressions.
explanations.d: ROSC is return of spontaneous circulation, a clinical state achieved during resuscitation rather than a coaching practice.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: During a resuscitation attempt, the rescuer providing compressions notices the person begins to breathe and cough. The team checks and feels a strong pulse. Which condition do these findings indicate?

answers.text: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia
Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC)
Agonal gasping without circulation
Foreign-body airway obstruction

explanations.a: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia by definition has no palpable pulse, so a strong pulse rules it out.
explanations.b: Breathing, coughing, or movement combined with a palpable pulse are signs of return of spontaneous circulation per AHA Part 4.
explanations.c: Agonal gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest, not recovery, and would not be paired with a strong pulse.
explanations.d: Airway obstruction would not produce a return of normal breathing and pulse during ongoing CPR.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: A patient achieves return of spontaneous circulation after in-hospital cardiac arrest and is moved to the cardiac catheterization lab. Which set of interventions best represents the AHA-recommended scope of post-cardiac arrest care?

answers.text: Hands-Only CPR continued for two more hours
Discharge home as soon as the pulse returns
Routine critical care support such as artificial ventilation, blood pressure management, and tailored therapies in the ED, cath lab, or intensive care unit
Only repeated AED rhythm checks every two minutes

explanations.a: Hands-Only CPR is for an arrest in progress; once ROSC is achieved, the focus shifts to advanced critical care.
explanations.b: Immediate discharge would skip the ventilation, blood pressure, and neurologic care that post-arrest patients require.
explanations.c: Per AHA Part 2, post-cardiac arrest care includes routine critical care support — ventilation, blood pressure management, and tailored therapies — in the ED, cath lab, or ICU.
explanations.d: Repeating AED analyses alone ignores the broader critical care needs that determine long-term survival.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: After a long, unsuccessful resuscitation attempt at a worksite, the team leader is reviewing AHA recovery and survivorship guidance with the rescuers. Which statement most accurately reflects that guidance?

answers.text: Psychological support and debriefing benefit rescuers and caregivers as well as survivors
Recovery support is only relevant for the patient, never for rescuers
Cardiac rehabilitation should be skipped to reduce health care costs
Family members of survivors should not be involved in recovery

explanations.a: AHA Part 2 explicitly notes rescuers and caregivers may benefit from psychological support, resiliency, burnout prevention, and effective debriefing.
explanations.b: The AHA approach extends recovery support beyond the patient to caregivers and rescuers as well.
explanations.c: Cardiac rehabilitation is a specific recommended intervention for many survivors and is not framed as optional based on cost.
explanations.d: Family members are part of the support network and AHA encourages a multimodal recovery approach including them.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: A nurse is preparing discharge teaching for a cardiac arrest survivor who had several minutes of downtime before bystander CPR. Which type of rehabilitation is specifically named by AHA recovery and survivorship guidance for survivors with brain-related deficits?

answers.text: Neurological recovery rehabilitation
Daily AED self-testing
Removal of the implanted cardioverter-defibrillator
Repeat public-access CPR training

explanations.a: AHA Part 2 explicitly states some patients need rehabilitation focused on neurological recovery in the survivorship phase.
explanations.b: Patients do not perform AED self-testing; that is a maintenance task for the device's owner or designated person.
explanations.c: Removing an implanted defibrillator is not part of routine recovery and would remove protection against future arrest.
explanations.d: Repeat CPR training is for rescuers, not for survivors recovering from neurological injury.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: A hospital quality committee is comparing how the Chain of Survival is applied inside the hospital versus on the street. Which characteristic distinguishes the in-hospital approach according to AHA Part 2?

answers.text: It relies primarily on lay rescuers locating a public AED
It does not include defibrillation as a link
It avoids advanced interventions to keep care simple
It focuses on prevention and early recognition through monitoring, with rapid response or medical emergency teams

explanations.a: Lay rescuer–and–public AED dependence describes the out-of-hospital setting, not in-hospital care.
explanations.b: Defibrillation remains a core link in both settings; the hospital simply uses monitor/defibrillators in addition to AEDs.
explanations.c: Hospitals are where advanced interventions like vascular access, medications, and advanced airways are most readily available.
explanations.d: AHA Part 2 says in-hospital care emphasizes prevention and early recognition with monitoring, supported by rapid response or medical emergency teams.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: An instructor reviews the AHA age definitions used throughout the BLS course. Which range correctly describes a 'child' for BLS purposes?

answers.text: From birth to 6 months of age
From 1 year of age to puberty
Anyone from 13 to 18 years of age only
Anyone older than puberty

explanations.a: Birth to 6 months falls within the infant category, not the child category.
explanations.b: AHA Part 1 defines a child as anyone from 1 year of age to the onset of puberty.
explanations.c: Adolescents who have reached puberty are treated as adults under BLS, not as children.
explanations.d: Anyone older than puberty is treated as an adult, not as a child.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.keyword: high quality CPR rate depth recoil
questions.text: A new lay rescuer asks the instructor what makes CPR most likely to keep someone alive until the AED arrives. Per the AHA, what is the single most important attribute of effective CPR?

answers.text: High-quality compressions performed at the correct rate, depth, and with full chest recoil
Loud encouragement shouted to the unresponsive person to wake them up
Carefully positioning the rescuer so the team leader can see the rescuer's face
Repeatedly checking for a pulse every 30 seconds during the resuscitation

explanations.a: AHA Part 2 emphasizes high-quality compressions — correct rate (100–120/min), depth (2–2.4 in for adults), and full recoil — as the foundation of effective CPR.
explanations.b: Verbal encouragement to the patient does not affect outcome; high-quality compressions and ventilations do.
explanations.c: Rescuer positioning relative to a leader is procedural, not the central determinant of CPR effectiveness.
explanations.d: Frequent pulse checks interrupt compressions and reduce coronary perfusion pressure; AHA limits pulse checks to ≤10 seconds and only when indicated.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.keyword: chain of survival OHCA IHCA links
questions.text: A community CPR class learns that the AHA publishes separate Chains of Survival for in-hospital and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. According to the AHA, why are the two chains different?

answers.text: Out-of-hospital arrests are always survivable while in-hospital arrests are not
The two settings have different rescuer types, resources, and pre-existing monitoring, so the link sequences differ
In-hospital CPR uses different compression depths than out-of-hospital CPR
Out-of-hospital chains skip defibrillation because AEDs are unavailable in the community

explanations.a: Both chains have survivors and non-survivors; the chains differ for systemic, not outcome-based, reasons.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2 explains that the in-hospital chain begins with surveillance and prevention because patients are already monitored, while the out-of-hospital chain begins with bystander recognition and 911 activation.
explanations.c: Compression depth (2–2.4 in for adults) is the same in both settings.
explanations.d: Public-access AEDs are widely available; defibrillation is a link in both chains.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.keyword: activate emergency response system AED request
questions.text: A bystander finds an adult collapsed on the floor of a busy office building. After confirming scene safety and unresponsiveness, what is the very next AHA-directed action before starting compressions?

answers.text: Begin compressions immediately and call for help only if the patient does not respond to CPR within 2 minutes
Move the patient to a private room before any further action to ensure dignity
Activate the emergency response system (call 911 or shout for help and ask someone to call) and request an AED
Place the patient in the recovery position and reassess in 30 seconds

explanations.a: Activating EMS before starting CPR ensures help is en route; do not delay the call to verify CPR works.
explanations.b: Moving the patient is not part of the recognition phase and may cause injury.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2: after recognizing unresponsiveness and abnormal/absent breathing, immediately activate the emergency response system and request an AED before starting compressions.
explanations.d: The recovery position is for breathing, responsive patients — not unresponsive ones suspected of arrest.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.keyword: public access defibrillation time to shock survival
questions.text: A workplace plans an AED program and the safety committee asks how AED placement affects survival from sudden cardiac arrest. According to AHA evidence cited in Part 3, which statement is correct?

answers.text: Public-access defibrillation has no measurable effect on survival rates because EMS arrives quickly enough in most areas
AEDs only help in hospitals; out-of-hospital use is discouraged
AEDs increase survival only when used by physicians
Time to defibrillation is the strongest single modifiable predictor of survival for shockable arrests; programs that shorten it improve survival rates

explanations.a: Public AED programs significantly improve survival, especially when placement reduces time-to-shock.
explanations.b: Out-of-hospital AED use by lay rescuers is encouraged and lifesaving; that is the purpose of public-access defibrillation.
explanations.c: AEDs are designed for use by trained lay rescuers, not exclusively physicians.
explanations.d: AHA Part 3 identifies time-to-defibrillation as a key modifiable factor; survival drops roughly 7–10% for every minute of delay without CPR.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: After ROSC is achieved on a 65-year-old in the field, the EMS team plans transport. According to AHA Part 4, which post-cardiac-arrest care priority most directly improves neurologic outcome?

answers.text: Targeted temperature management and avoidance of hypotension and hypoxemia during the post-arrest period
Immediate administration of dextrose to all post-arrest patients regardless of glucose level
Withholding all fluids until the patient is fully awake
Routine therapeutic hypothermia to a core temperature of 28°C

explanations.a: AHA Part 4 highlights targeted temperature management (32–36°C), avoidance of hypotension, and maintenance of normoxia/normocapnia as core post-arrest priorities.
explanations.b: Dextrose is given only for documented hypoglycemia, not routinely.
explanations.c: Hemodynamic support, including fluids when indicated, is part of post-arrest care.
explanations.d: Targeted temperature is 32–36°C, not 28°C; deeper hypothermia is not recommended.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.keyword: recovery survivorship multimodal rehab mental health
questions.text: A cardiac arrest survivor and family are being discharged from the hospital after ROSC and successful neurologic recovery. According to AHA recovery guidance, what comprehensive support should be offered?

answers.text: Discharge with no follow-up because survival itself is the goal
Multimodal rehabilitation including physical, cognitive, and emotional support, plus screening for anxiety/depression in survivors and family
Only cardiology follow-up; cognitive symptoms resolve spontaneously and do not need attention
Mandatory long-term institutionalization regardless of recovery

explanations.a: AHA Part 4 recovery guidance emphasizes multimodal post-discharge support, not just survival.
explanations.b: AHA recovery framework calls for physical, cognitive, and emotional rehabilitation, plus mental health screening for survivors and family — recovery is its own link in the Chain of Survival.
explanations.c: Cognitive deficits, fatigue, and PTSD-like symptoms are common after arrest and need active screening and treatment.
explanations.d: Most survivors return to community living; institutionalization is not a default.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.text: An ICU nurse and a community lay rescuer compare their roles during cardiac arrest. According to AHA, which statement most accurately distinguishes the two settings?

answers.text: Both use identical equipment, training, and response procedures
Lay rescuers in the community administer the same medications as in-hospital teams

In-hospital arrests benefit from continuous monitoring, immediate code-team response, and advanced equipment, while out-of-hospital arrests rely first on bystander CPR and public AEDs until EMS arrives
Out-of-hospital cardiac arrests cannot be treated with defibrillation

explanations.a: Equipment and training differ substantially between settings.
explanations.b: Lay rescuers do not administer cardiac arrest medications; that is the role of advanced providers.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2: the two chains begin with different first links because of available resources — surveillance/prevention in-hospital vs. bystander recognition out-of-hospital.
explanations.d: Public-access AEDs allow defibrillation in the out-of-hospital setting before EMS arrival.

questions.name: Introduction and Chain of Survival
questions.keyword: child age definition puberty AHA Part 6
questions.text: A new student studying CPR asks how the AHA defines "child" for the purposes of pediatric BLS. According to AHA Part 6, which definition applies?

answers.text: Child means anyone under 21 years of age
Child means anyone weighing less than 50 kg regardless of age
Child means anyone with a heart rate under 100 bpm
Child means age 1 year through the onset of puberty (signs of puberty such as breast development in females, axillary hair in males)

explanations.a: AHA pediatric definitions are age-based with a puberty threshold, not a 21-year cutoff.
explanations.b: Pediatric BLS uses age and physical-development criteria, not weight thresholds for age categorization.
explanations.c: Heart rate is part of clinical assessment, not age categorization.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 defines child as age 1 year through puberty; infant is under 1 year (excluding newborns at delivery).
